introduction: The review aims to investigate the effects of chronic exercise on overall depression severity and on different symptoms of depression in older adults, in randomized controlled trials, including the moderating effects of intervention and individual characteristics. The authors state that, to their knowledge, no published review or meta-analysis has examined the broadest possible range of symptoms.
methodology: Protocol for a systematic and meta-analytical review of randomized controlled trials of chronic exercise in older adults, following PRISMA-P. Eligible studies are RCTs with parallel-group or cluster designs and a mean age of 60 years or above. Several databases will be searched from inception. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection, data extraction and quality assessment. A random-effects model will be used, with Hedges' g as the effect size, and GRADE and RoB2 will assess quality.
results: The paper is a protocol and reports no results.
discussion: The authors expect a moderate effect of exercise on depression compared with active and passive control groups, and expect the results to be moderated by intervention and individual characteristics. They state that the conclusions may serve as a basis for evidence-based recommendations for individualized exercise programs. They also suggest that the review results may reveal research gaps for further RCTs.
limitations: The authors note that, because RCTs with pharmacological or psychotherapy effects are excluded, no conclusions can be drawn for exercise as add-on treatment, and that they may miss some clinically relevant insights. They anticipate heterogeneous data and wide variance in how exercise and individual characteristics are reported. They suggest the review may show whether comorbidities or physical fitness level still require further research.

introduction.q: the objective of the proposed review is to investigate the effects of chronic exercise on overall depression severity and on different symptoms of depression in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) including older adults with a mean age of at least 60 years
and by considering the moderating effects of intervention characteristics and individual characteristics
to our knowledge, there is no published review or meta-analysis that attempts to uncover the effects of chronic exercise on the broadest possible range of symptoms as described in the DSM

methodology.q: In this article, we have outlined a protocol for a systematic and meta-analytical review
follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocol (PRISMA-P) statement
Eligible studies only include RCTs with either a parallel-group design
the mean age of each arm of the RCT is 60 years or above
Our review further aims to encompass all populations of older adults independent of disease
The intervention must last at least one week and include more than one exercise session.

The following electronic databases will be searched from inception to shortly before publishing the meta-analysis: Web of Science (all bases); Academic Search Complete, MEDLINE with full text, CINAHL with full text, APA Psycinfo, SPORTDiscuss with full text through EBSCO host; Cochrane.

results.q: In this article, we have outlined a protocol for a systematic and meta-analytical review on the effects of chronic exercise on depression in older adults
This protocol has been published in the Prospero repository

discussion.q: we expect to find a moderate effect of exercise on depression compared to active and passive control groups with no exercise components
We further expect the results to be moderated by intervention characteristics and individual characteristics
the conclusions drawn from this review may serve as a basis for developing evidence-based recommendations for individualized exercise programs that can help alleviate depression in older adults
the review results may reveal research gaps that can stimulate the formulation of research questions for further RCTs

limitations.q: We plan to exclude RCTs with tested effects of pharmacological treatment and / or psychotherapy.
Therefore, no conclusions can be drawn for exercise interventions as add-on treatment.
We are aware that by that we might miss some clinically relevant insights.
We further anticipate limitations in form of heterogenous data and a wide variance in the reporting of the exercise characteristics (e.g., detailedness) and the individual characteristics.
For instance, it can reveal whether certain moderator variables, such as comorbidities or physical fitness level still require further research to understand their influence.

abstract_claims.q: There is high evidence that chronic exercise benefits overall depression severity in older adults.
The results of the proposed review are anticipated to have a substantial impact on research and clinical practice.
On the one hand, the review’s conclusions could form the foundation for developing evidence-based recommendations for individualized exercise programs that alleviate depression in older adults.
by revealing research gaps, the review results could encourage the formulation of research questions for further RCTs.

caveats.q: However, the heterogeneity of the effects is high, which might be caused by variations between exercise interventions.
